pages.text: On careers day, Kwao’s class listed jobs they wanted: doctor, engineer, pilot. Then someone asked Kwao’s cousin Elinam, who had come to speak, what she did. “I farm vegetables,” she said. Kwao snorted. “Farming is for people who failed school,” he muttered. The room went quiet. Elinam only smiled. “Come to my farm on Saturday,” she said. “Then tell me what you think.”

pages.alt: A boy with folded arms sits in a classroom while a young woman in a sun hat speaks.

pages.text: On Saturday, Elinam met him in a green field and handed him her phone. “This tells me the weather for the week,” she said, “so I know when to plant and when to cover the beds.” She showed him an app with market prices. According to an article from 2026, platforms such as AgroCenta and Farmerline give farmers prices, weather forecasts and advice, and some help them sell directly to buyers. “Features and fees differ,” Elinam added. “I check before I trust any of them.”

pages.alt: A young woman shows a boy a phone with a weather forecast and prices in a vegetable field.

pages.text: Elinam told him what the same article reports. In the north, young maize and soybean farmers use phone apps to plan planting around the rain forecast. In the south, some young cocoa farmers use digital monitoring to spot pests early. In the Ashanti Region, a cooperative of young vegetable farmers sells pesticide-free produce to supermarkets in Accra, using cold-chain transport. In the Volta Region, young poultry farmers use feed calculations to cut costs. “The article does not give proof for each one,” she said, “so I treat them as reports.”

pages.text: Kwao’s eyebrows lifted. “And the old miners?” he asked, because his uncle had mined. Elinam nodded. “In 2023, a municipal agriculture director in the Eastern Region told the Minerals Commission board that about three thousand former small-scale illegal miners had become oil palm farmers, with more than four hundred thousand seedlings given out since 2020. But the seedlings went only to people who had farmland, one beneficiary asked for a palm-processing factory, and it is too early to know the long-term result.”

pages.alt: A young woman holds a palm seedling beside rows of young oil palm trees in a field.

pages.text: “And the style?” Kwao asked, looking at her neat shed. “Farming is a business,” said Elinam. “I grade my vegetables, pack them in clean crates, put a label with my name and phone number on each one, and keep records. Some young people are even learning to fly drones over farms, according to news reports. People pay for good quality and for trust.” Kwao looked at the shed. “It does not look like what I imagined,” he admitted. “Most people imagine a cutlass and a tired back,” Elinam said. “There is some of that too.”

pages.text: She grew serious. “I will not lie to you,” said Elinam. “One year, heavy rain washed away a whole bed of peppers. Prices drop when many farmers harvest at once. Land is hard to get, and so is money. Many young people give up in the first two years.” Kwao swallowed. “So how do you stay?” he asked. “I started small, I learnt from older farmers, I joined a group, and I keep trying new things,” she said. “It is not magic. It is work, with brains.”

pages.text: On Monday, Mrs Boampong, the English teacher, set a descriptive task: describe a place you know. Kwao wrote: “At six o’clock the field glowed green under the golden sun. The air smelt of wet soil and fresh leaves, and a gentle wind rustled the neat rows like whispering paper. Cousin Elinam’s hands, rough but steady, laid crisp lettuce in a clean crate. The cool water pipe ticked softly as it dripped. I tasted a sweet tomato, and it burst on my tongue like a tiny sunrise.”

I tasted a sweet tomato, and it burst on my tongue like a tiny sunrise.”
pages.alt: A boy writes a descriptive paragraph at his desk with a green field drawn in the margin.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: a descriptive paragraph uses the five senses (sight, sound, smell, taste and touch), strong adjectives, and comparisons such as similes and metaphors. Kwao wrote in the past tense and avoided slang and contractions. He also showed rather than told: he did not say “it was beautiful”, he described what made it so. Change your first opinion if the facts change, as Kwao did. The end.
